topic_name: Making Symmetric Shapes: Ink, Folds and Cuts

item.question: Take a piece of paper and fold it in half. Open it and spill a few drops of ink (or paint) on one half. Press the halves together and open the paper again. What do you see? Is the resulting figure symmetric? If yes, where is the line of symmetry? Is there any other line along which it can be folded to produce two identical parts? Try making more such patterns.
steps: Fold the paper in half and put ink on one half.
Press the halves together and open: the ink prints a mirror image on the other half.
The crease is the line of symmetry.
item.answer: You see a blot pattern with the same shape on both sides of the crease. Yes, it is symmetric and the fold (crease) is the line of symmetry. Usually no other line works, since the shape is random, so there is just one line of symmetry.

item.question: Look at the rangoli picture (a round flower-like design with a ring in the centre and four red petals around it). Can you see what repeats in it? What happens to the red petals when the rangoli is rotated by 90° around the centre?
steps: Look at the red petals around the centre.
Turn the picture by 90° (a quarter turn) about the centre.
Each petal lands exactly on the next petal, so the pattern repeats.
item.answer: The same petal shape repeats around the centre. When the rangoli is turned by 90° about its centre, the red petals come back exactly onto themselves, and so do the other parts.

item.question: A paper windmill with 4 equal blades looks the same when turned by 90° about the red point at its centre. Will the windmill look exactly the same when rotated through an angle of less than 90°?
steps: Turn the windmill by a small angle, say 45°.
The blades do not land on the blades again.
The first turn that makes it look the same is 90°, so no smaller angle works.

topic_name: Rotational Symmetry and Angles of Symmetry
concept_name: The windmill and its centre of rotation

item.question: The windmill has exactly 4 angles of symmetry: 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°. Do you know of any other shape that has exactly four angles of symmetry?
steps: A shape with 4 angles of symmetry matches itself after each quarter turn.
A square does this: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°.
A plus sign with 4 equal arms does the same.
item.answer: Yes, a square (also a plus sign made of 4 equal arms, or a pinwheel with 4 equal blades).

3. A plus sign with 4 equal arms does the same.
Answer: Yes, a square (also a plus sign made of 4 equal arms, or a pinwheel with 4 equal blades).

topic_name: Rotational Symmetry and Angles of Symmetry
concept_name: The square: four angles of symmetry

item.question: How many angles of symmetry does a square have? How much rotation does it require to get the initial square?
steps: Rotate the square about its centre by a quarter turn: it overlaps itself.
Each further quarter turn does the same: 90°, 180°, 270°.
A full turn of 360° brings every corner back to its own place.
item.answer: 4 angles of symmetry: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°. The square overlaps itself after a 90° rotation (A goes to B, B to C, C to D, D to A); it is back in its starting position after 360°.

Answer: 4 angles of symmetry: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°. The square overlaps itself after a 90° rotation (A goes to B, B to C, C to D, D to A); it is back in its starting position after 360°.

item.question: A square gets back onto itself after a 90° rotation. Do you know where to mark the centre of rotation?
steps: The centre of rotation is the fixed point that does not move.
In a square this is the middle point.
It is where the diagonals meet.
